question: Xi Jinping out before 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if China's General Secretary of the Communist Party, Xi Jinping, is removed from power for any length of time between July 3, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping will be considered removed from power if he announces his resignation from his role as General Secretary, or is otherwise dismissed, detained, disqualified, or otherwise loses his position or is prevented from fulfilling his duties as General Secretary within this market's timeframe.

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

eventMetadata.context_description: Xi Jinping's consolidated authority within the Chinese Communist Party, reinforced by the 2018 removal of presidential term limits and his third-term confirmation at the 2020 National Congress, underpins trader consensus that he will remain in power through 2026. The upcoming 21st Party Congress scheduled for late 2027 is widely anticipated to extend his leadership into a fourth term, with no verified challenges, elite fractures, or succession signals emerging in recent months. Analysts note that institutional mechanisms and party discipline continue to favor continuity absent major disruption. Realistic factors that could still shift probabilities include sudden health developments, severe economic downturns triggering elite dissatisfaction, or unforeseen external crises prompting internal reevaluation before the congress.

eventMetadata.context_description: The tight race for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination reflects an early, open field more than two years before any declarations or formal primary contests. Trader consensus currently prices Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Gov. Gavin Newsom, and Sen. Jon Ossoff as the clearest early leaders, with the remaining field fragmented across governors, senators, and other national figures. Recent DNC approval of a revised primary calendar beginning with South Carolina and Nevada has highlighted the importance of diverse voter coalitions, while ongoing Senate primaries in states such as Michigan and Minnesota serve as early tests of party messaging on populism and electability. With no candidate yet committing and historical patterns showing rapid shifts once the invisible primary intensifies, small changes in polling, endorsements, or perceived viability could quickly widen or narrow these gaps.
